summary:
Malta decriminalised same-sex conduct on 29 January 1973 and now operates one of the strongest legal frameworks for transgender people in its regional bloc. On 15 April 2014 parliament approved a constitutional amendment naming gender identity as a protected ground, the first European state to do so, and introduced civil unions in the same sitting. Statutory discrimination protections extend to sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics, and legal gender recognition requires no surgery. Nonbinary identity is recognised, and hate-crime provisions cover sexual-orientation and gender-identity offences.

Rules governing everyday access are settled rather than contested: same-sex marriage since 2017, full joint adoption since 2014, open military service, protected bathroom access, a ban on conversion therapy and a full ban on intersex infant surgery. Equaldex records no restrictions on legal gender change and reports that 84% of respondents consider the country a good place for gay people.

Physical risk to visitors is low. A 2025 academic chapter in the Routledge Companion to Gender and Crime, by Mary Grace Vella, records one of the lowest rates of physical or sexual victimisation of LGBTIQ+ people among the 27 EU member states, and the Malta Police Force operates hate-crime procedures for sexual-orientation and gender-identity incidents. The same research finds that non-physical harassment and online hatred make up a comparatively larger share of what LGBTIQ+ people experience, and that reporting of violence to the Malta Police Force remains significantly low despite institutional reform.

Border handling is the sharpest documented exposure. In M.S. v. Malta, an LGBTI asylum seeker was detained on arrival in April 2023 and served with a return decision and removal order to Bangladesh in May 2024; on 30 July 2025 the International Commission of Jurists and partner organisations filed observations at the European Court of Human Rights raising non-refoulement under Article 3, detention conditions and the absence of an individualised assessment before detention under Articles 5 and 13. The case concerns an asylum seeker rather than a visa-holding traveller, but it is direct evidence of how an LGBTI arrival can be screened, held and ordered removed.

Detention inside the country is the weakest documented point. On 29 May 2018 the Maltese civil court, Judge Silvio Meli, awarded seven transgender inmates of Corradino prison €5,000 each after prison authorities held them in the male section, where they shared cells with male inmates, used the men's showers and were subjected to insults and what the proceedings described as continuous sexual abuse and violence. The court found that the authorities had knowingly and repeatedly placed the women in situations of high risk of sexual and psychological violence; the only alternative offered, transfer to the female section, would have cost them the work and study opportunities they needed to pay for hormone therapy, and warders and inmates there were hostile. The director of prisons was ordered to pay, with the Aditus Foundation representing the seven women.

A 2024 University of Malta dissertation by Oriana Vidal, drawing on interviews with four current and former transgender and gender-diverse inmates of the Correctional Service Agency across a 25-year cohort, finds that agency practice, policies and procedures lag the national gender-identity law: participants now hold individual cells in the female section but report residual misgendering by officers using masculine birth names, along with gaps in gender-appropriate clothing and healthcare, and the study records problems after release as well as deficiencies in healthcare, legislation and staff knowledge.

Social climate is the remaining caution. Despite the legal position, Maltese respondents rank first of 30 EU regions for hiding being LGBTIQ at work, and harassment and online hatred remain more prevalent than physical violence.
